headline: Chris Judd highlights Firmus as a key enabler of the Australian data centre build-out, backed by Nvidia and planning to list on ASX

The key risk to Ma's Group's thesis is Firmus's ability to secure full funding and execute on its capacity plans, though Judd notes Ma's does not require Firmus to list — only that it remains funded and able to lease capacity.
quote: Firmus are planning to build 3.3GW of capacity in Australia alone for every one gigawatt of capacity, that's around $2 billion worth of revenue that goes to jail Group or Ma's group as the parent entity... if you look at firmus, you know they're already backed by Nvidia, who recently wrote out a $500 million check to fund them. They've been able to raise considerable, considerable amount of funding so far. But certainly if firmus wasn't able to list and wasn't able to get their required funding, that'd be the most obvious risk to Mars group.

headline: Chris Judd sees AI data centre CapEx as the most significant macro trend since China joined the WTO, with multi-year tailwinds for second and third order beneficiaries
reasoning: Judd argues the data centre CapEx cycle is the most significant macro trend since China entered the WTO in 2000. He believes calling it a bubble is premature, and that the scale of capital to be deployed will underwrite the value of electrical engineering groups, HVAC installers and other second and third order beneficiaries for many years. He also highlights national security implications of allowing data centre capacity to be built offshore rather than domestically.
quote: I think you have had plenty of people come on and talk about both AI and the data center CapEx cycle that we were in and how significant it is. But from our perspective, we think it's the most significant macro trend since China entered the WTO at the, um, you know, the year 2000. And we think whilst many of the companies involved have had significant gains already, we think calling it a bubble is calling it way too early, and particularly from a data center CapEx side of things. We think the amount of capital that's going to be spent is going to underwrite the value of the electrical engineering groups, the HVAC installers, and many of the other second and third order beneficiaries of that spend for many years to come.

headline: Chris Judd bullish on Mars Group as data centre CapEx buildout drives demand for specialist power cube manufacturing
reasoning: Mars Group is not just doing general electrical engineering for data centres — they have a unique capability in factory-manufacturing 'power cubes' off-site before transporting them to data centre sites, ahead of final installation by others. This specialised skill set is difficult to replicate and positions Mars well regardless of the fate of anchor client Firmus. While Firmus failing to list or secure funding would be the most obvious risk to Mars, the broader data centre CapEx buildout remains enormous and Mars's services would still be in demand from other groups. The combination of a unique product, a structural growth tailwind, and limited competition in this niche makes Mars a compelling small cap holding.
quote: Not just Mars aren't just doing general electrical engineering work for the data centers. They've actually got involved in factory manufacturing of the process, where they build what's called a power cube off, off site, and then transport that to the data center before other groups do that final installation piece. That's quite a unique, specific skill that that Mars have and do. So even if firmus weren't to be able to execute on their full gigawatt capacity plans, we still think there's other groups that will be able to use Mars's services.

headline: Chris Judd sees mining and data centre CapEx as the two main private sector job creation drivers in the Australian economy going forward
reasoning: Judd argues that outside of mining and data centre construction, almost all other job creation in Australia will come from the public sector, including the NDIS and government initiatives. He believes the Australian government will ultimately support the data centre theme due to its job creation potential, and stresses that allowing data centres to be built offshore carries serious national security implications including grid vulnerability.
quote: I think if you look at the Australian economy now, um, you know, we think mining is going to be relatively strong in terms of jobs created. And we think datacentre CapEx is going to be strong in terms of jobs created and almost very little else in the private sector. I think all the other job creation in Australia is going to come from or not. All the vast majority of it will be come from the public service and things like the NDIS and government initiatives. So even whilst, you know, the Australian government might be not as quick to to maybe realise the value of these trends, I think they're going to be able to understand the importance of the jobs that can get created here.

Um, and you know, we think the earnings season has been strong enough. We think it's more expectations were really low. We think there's been a good bounce in the small. You know this month that's been particularly strong. But we still think there's a considerable catch up between Australian small caps and us small caps. headline: Ceruti Macro Fund bullish on Generation Development Group after strong FY26 result demonstrates excessive pessimism was priced in

headline: Ceruti Macro Fund believes ASX small cap selloff is overdone with green shoots emerging
reasoning: Chris Judd argues that the selloff in Australian small caps was driven by budget-related pessimism from the Albanese government's fiscal announcements, which hurt market confidence and liquidity at the smaller end. He observes a divergence between the Russell 2000 in the US (which has been stronger) and Australian small caps, suggesting Australian stocks have catch-up potential. The strong one-day re-rating in GDG, where the stock rose ~35% on results that merely met expectations, illustrates how much pessimism was priced into quality small caps.
quote: We think the sell off, particularly in Aussie small caps is now overdone. We think that was largely based around the budget, which Comrade Chalmers and Comrade Alvanese, announced a couple of months ago, and which really set the market of confidence and the market of liquidity in the smaller end of the market. But we're seeing a discrepancy or divergence between, say, the Russell 2000, the US, which are their small stocks and the Australian stocks. We now feel there's an ability for our stocks to catch up.

headline: Ceruti Macro Fund bullish on Medallion as a fully funded near-term gold and copper producer with significant upside
reasoning: Chris Judd likes Medallion because it acquired the Cosmic Boy processing plant from IGO for zero upfront cost, gaining infrastructure including grid power, camps, and ore processing facilities, in exchange for taking on ~$70M in rehabilitation liability and a 1.5% NSR. The company is fully funded with no further dilution expected before production ramp-up and is currently milling third-party ore to test the plant. At a ~$350M market cap, Judd estimates the plant alone is worth ~$200M. A life-of-mine extension via drilling would be a major re-rating catalyst, and even without it he considers the stock very cheap.
quote: Medallion is one that we really like. It's fully funded. It's a near-term producer. They bought some assets of IDO and largely they bought the Cosmic Boy processing plant. What made it such an incredible deal, it was for zero money upfront. And they got forestation, they got grid power, they got camps, etc. They'll take on that rehabilitation liability, which is about, let's call it $70M and an NSR about 1.5% over the production from that facility. But like I said, fully funded, they shouldn't be any more dilution between now and when they ramp up into production. It's going to be incredibly cheap on a two-year basis if they get anywhere near nameplate capacity. And we just think it's one of those positions where not much is built into it... The one caveat, it's got sort of a five, just under six-year life of mine currently. We think that can be extended with some drilling. There's an enormous rerate coming if they were able to extend that life of mine. And even if they don't, we think it's incredibly cheap here.

headline: Ceruti Macro Fund sees gold selloff as temporary, bull case intact with bottom in place

And everywhere we look, we still say that the bull case for gold is intact, albeit it's been caught up with this momentum sell off that we think a bottom is in, and it's time for a rebound, which we started to see over the last week or so.

headline: Ceruti Macro Fund views momentum stock selloff as indiscriminate and driven by South Korean margin unwind

headline: Ceruti Macro Fund takes contrarian view that next RBA move is not a hike, citing underemployment and property market weakness
reasoning: Despite the stronger-than-expected June jobs numbers, Chris Judd is not convinced the RBA's next move will be a rate hike, even though that is current consensus. He points to underemployment as a significant ongoing issue, weakness in the Victorian property market, and notes that the federal government's budgetary policies and tax increases are already performing the demand-dampening role that rate hikes would otherwise play. He believes the government's fiscal tightening effectively substitutes for monetary tightening.
quote: Rate hikes will be a negative. We'll probably take the other side of that bet. I'm not convinced that the next move will be up in Australia. I'm aware that that is currently consensus. We still think underemployment is a significant issue. We're seeing the property market roll over. Certainly the jobs numbers in Victoria were absolutely horrendous and unemployment rose locally, which would be a market the RBA would be concerned about. And to be honest, we think a lot of the heavy lifting that the RBA would normally do is currently being done by the federal government and some of their budgetary policies and tax increases, which we think will hurt the demand, similar to what rate rises would.

headline: Structural shift toward energy security and supply chain redundancy seen as persistent inflationary tailwind regardless of Iran war outcome
reasoning: Chris Judd argues that irrespective of whether the Iran conflict ends or continues, countries and businesses will increasingly prioritise energy security, critical minerals stockpiling, and supply chain redundancy. He believes this represents a paradigm shift rather than a temporary phenomenon, paving the way for a more inflationary environment. Transportation of energy and minerals is expected to become less smooth, and both companies and nations will hold greater commodity stockpiles than before. National security as a structural investment theme is expected to persist.
quote: I think, like you said, everyone's hoping to an end to the conflict in Iran, obviously for humanitarian reasons, but from for market reasons also. But I do think no matter what happens from here, we're still going to see some things remain around energy security, around countries wanting to put their foot on critical minerals, and countries and businesses not wanting to rely on supply chains that are just in time and very much have much more redundancy built into their supply chain. So we feel it's paving the way for a more inflationary environment going forward. An environment where, you know, the transportation of energy and minerals is not as smooth as it once was. And a world where companies and countries alike feel they need greater stockpiles of commodities and critical things to run their businesses and their countries than they did before. And we don't think that's going to change whether or not the war keeps going or whether or not it ends tomorrow.
